standards.title: Shared Standards Across Tools
standards.intro: In December 2025 the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) launched under the Linux Foundation, with MCP, AGENTS.md, and goose donated as founding projects. Learn the standards that aren't tied to one tool and you can carry your setup and knowledge with you when the tool changes.

example.title: Handing a Task to an Agent
example.promptCode:
# Start an interactive session with an initial prompt
claude "Implement user authentication:
       - JWT auth with refresh tokens
       - Login/logout API
       - Login form component
       Done when: bun run typecheck and bun run test pass"
steps: Explore the project structure and existing patterns
Create/modify the files it needs
Run type checks and tests
On failure, read the cause and fix again
Report once the done criteria are met

usageLadder.description: Use each step well, and move up only when you can see its limit.
usageLadder.notice: This is based on official docs and GitHub repositories checked on 2026-11-10. Tools change every few months, so re-check commands in each official doc before using them. Prices and benchmark rankings are not covered.
usageLadder.principleBody: Use one step thoroughly, and move to the next only when you can see that step's limit. Running more agents does not give better results. When the checking work (review, tests) piles up on one person, things get slower.

s1.title: ① Simple use: conversational questions and single tasks
s1.does: Ask for an explanation of the codebase, paste an error message and ask for the cause, or have it fix one function. The Claude Code docs use questions like "give me an overview of this codebase" and "how is authentication handled?".
habits: Give the reproduction command together with the full error.
Point at files directly, like @src/utils/auth.js (the Claude Code @ reference).
Repeat small, verifiable requests instead of one big request.
s1.when: If you keep typing the same explanation ("this project uses bun and kebab-case") three or more times, go to ②.
mistakes: Committing the result without reading it.
Piling unrelated tasks into one conversation and cluttering the context.

s2.title: ② Project instruction files and reusable procedures (skills)
s2.rulesLead: A rule file holds "facts that always apply". The file name differs by tool.

rows: CLAUDE.md (v2.1.277 and later also read AGENTS.md when CLAUDE.md is absent, see below)
AGENTS.md (global: ~/.codex/AGENTS.md; in a repo: root or subdirectories; the file closest to the working directory wins)
GEMINI.md (see "Note on the Google family" in step ⑥)

s2.rulesNote: If you mix tools, it is convenient to keep the shared rules in a single AGENTS.md. The official docs confirm that Copilot reads AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and GEMINI.md, and that Codex reads AGENTS.md.
s2.claudeAgentsBody: According to the official Claude Code docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory), v2.1.277 and later read the repository's AGENTS.md as project instructions when there is no CLAUDE.md. If both exist, only CLAUDE.md is read. To use both, import AGENTS.md from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md.
s2.skillsLead: A skill holds a "procedure loaded only when needed". Write the description and step-by-step instructions in a SKILL.md file. Only the description is always in context; the body loads when the skill is invoked.
s2.skillPathsCode:
# Claude Code
.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md      project (commit to the repo to share)
~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md    personal

# Codex
.agents/skills                            repository
~/.agents/skills                          personal
s2.skillFileCode:
---
name: summarize-changes
description: Summarizes uncommitted changes and flags anything risky. Use when the user asks what changed or wants a commit message.
---
s2.skillUse: In Claude Code you can call a skill directly, like /summarize-changes, or Claude loads it automatically when your request matches the description. For procedures with side effects, such as deployment, use disable-model-invocation: true. The Claude Code docs advise moving a CLAUDE.md section into a skill once it has become a multi-step procedure rather than a fact.
s2.when: If the agent still "fixes things right away without a plan and breaks them" after you tidy the instructions, go to ③.
mistakes: Growing the instruction file to hundreds of lines. The Codex docs also say to keep AGENTS.md small.
Leaving the instructions out of sync with the real repository (script names, directories).
Assuming the team can use a skill that exists only on your own PC. The Cursor docs explain that local skills that are not synced are not copied to cloud agents.

s3.title: ③ Plan first, then execute, and the verification loop
s3.planLead: Plan first. In Claude Code plan mode, it reads files and only proposes a plan, and it does not edit anything before you approve.
s3.planNote: During a session you can press Shift+Tab to switch to plan mode. Cursor also switches to Plan Mode with Shift+Tab in the chat input, and Antigravity CLI has a /plan command. For a tool without a planning feature, ask "do not edit code; write only a step-by-step plan first" instead.
s3.verifyLead: The verification loop. Give the agent a way to check its own work. State the following in the instruction file.
s3.verifyCode:
After every change, always run: bun run typecheck, bun run lint, bun run test
If anything fails, fix the cause and run again. Do not say the task is done before they pass.
s3.headlessLead: Non-interactive runs can also serve the verification loop. An example from the Claude Code docs:
s3.headlessCode: git log --oneline -20 | claude -p "summarize these recent commits"
s3.hookNote: Claude Code hooks (such as TaskCompleted) can also automate a rule that blocks marking a task complete before tests pass. This hook was confirmed in the agent teams docs.
s3.when: If planning and verification work well but research or review quickly fills the main context, go to ④.
mistakes: Approving the plan without reading it.
Trusting the agent's "verified" claim in areas with no tests. An agent may also edit the tests to make them pass, so check test file changes in the diff.

s4.title: ④ Delegation inside one session: subagents
s4.lead: A subagent is a helper with its own context window. You hand it the bulk file reading and get back only a summary, so the main conversation stays clean. An example from the Claude Code docs:
s4.promptCode: use a subagent to investigate how our auth system handles token refresh
s4.locationsLead: The definition file location differs by tool.

rows: .claude/agents/*.md, ~/.claude/agents/*.md (YAML frontmatter + body as the system prompt)
Standalone TOML files in .codex/agents/ and ~/.codex/agents/ (name, description, developer_instructions required)

s4.exampleLead: A Claude Code example. Only name and description are required.
s4.exampleCode:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices. Use proactively after code changes.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet
---

You are a code reviewer. Analyze the code and provide specific,
actionable feedback on quality, security, and best practices.
s4.notes: Codex tells you to request subagents or parallel work explicitly (for example "spawn two agents"), and in the CLI you switch between active threads with /subagents. The number of concurrent threads is limited by agents.max_concurrent_threads_per_session. Cursor supports the readonly and is_background keys in frontmatter.
s4.when: A subagent is bound to the lifetime and context of one session. To work on different features at the same time for a long while, go to ⑤.
mistakes: Letting several subagents edit the same file.
Granting write access even for read-only work (research, review). Block it with the tools allow list or readonly.
Leaving context out of the delegation prompt. Assume a subagent does not inherit the conversation history and write down what it needs.

s5.title: ⑤ Parallel sessions: worktrees, background, cloud
s5.worktreeLead: A git feature that checks out several branches of one repository into separate directories at the same time. It is used to give each agent its own working directory.
s5.worktreeCode:
git worktree add -b feature-a ../myapp-feature-a
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../myapp-feature-a
s5.toolLead: Tools can also do this for you.
s5.toolCode:
# Claude Code: run it with another name in a second terminal for an isolated parallel session
claude --worktree feature-auth
s5.cursorNote: Cursor creates a separate checkout per agent in the Agents Window, and in the IDE you use the /worktree, /best-of-n, /apply-worktree, and /delete-worktree commands. Write the setup steps for a new worktree under the setup-worktree-unix, setup-worktree-windows, and setup-worktree keys in .cursor/worktrees.json. A Claude Code subagent runs in a temporary worktree if you put isolation: worktree in its frontmatter.
s5.caution: A worktree separates only the working files. Dev server ports, databases, and dependency installs such as node_modules must be managed separately. (The Cursor docs do not recommend symlinking dependencies and recommend fast package managers such as bun, pnpm, and uv.)
s5.bgLead: The docs say the Claude Code agent view is a research preview and its interface may change.
s5.bgCode:
claude --bg "investigate the flaky SettingsChangeDetector test"
claude agents            # show all background sessions on one screen
claude attach <id>       # attach to a session
claude logs <id>
claude stop <id>
s5.bgStates: Session states are shown as Working, Needs input, Idle, Completed, Failed, and Stopped. You can send a running conversation to the background with /bg.
cloud: The GitHub Copilot cloud agent researches the repository, plans, and runs file edits and tests in the background in a cloud development environment. It works with one branch and one PR per task.
Claude Code offers cloud scheduled tasks (routines). They run even when your computer is off and are set up at claude.ai/code/routines.
The Cursor docs say subagents can also be used in Cloud Agents.

The Codex docs include an example of delegating work to a cloud chat by adding @codex ... to a PR comment. Codex Cloud gives each task its own workspace and keeps running while your computer is asleep; you review changes from the web, mobile, or desktop app, then commit or open a pull request. An environment must be published before you can start a new task.
s5.when: When you have more than three or four sessions and start spending time finding which session is waiting for input, consider ⑥.
mistakes: Running tasks that touch the same files in parallel and causing merge conflicts. Split the work by file ownership.
Forgetting to clean up worktrees until the disk fills. Cursor uses 25 as the default machine-wide limit and can automatically clean up old worktrees (cursor.worktreeMaxCount).
Trying to review all parallel results at once and creating a bottleneck. The speed at which a person can review is the upper limit.

s6.title: ⑥ Multi-agent orchestration
kinds: Built-in team features of an agent. A single agent product builds a team.
External tools that wrap agents. A terminal runtime (herdr) or a desktop app (Orca) runs and manages many kinds of agents in one place.
s6.teamsTitle: Built-in teams: Claude Code agent teams
s6.teamsLead: An experimental feature that is off by default. Turn it on with an environment variable.
s6.teamsNote: A team lead session creates teammates (independent Claude Code sessions) and coordinates through a shared task list and messages between teammates. The docs recommend 3 to 5 teammates to start and suggest beginning with work that writes no code, such as review and research. The docs also list limits: one team per session, no nested teams, and far more token use than subagents. Split-pane mode needs tmux or iTerm2 (the --teammate-mode flag).
s6.whenLabel: When to move up (and when not to)
when: Move up when you have several independent tasks, each with automatic verification (tests), and time to review.
If the tasks are sequential or touch the same files a lot, ④ or a single session is better. The Claude Code docs say the same.
mistakes: Making "run many agents" the goal itself.
Leaving several agents unsupervised with all permissions allowed (such as --dangerously-skip-permissions). The docs say that in Claude Code teams, teammates inherit the lead's permission mode.
Treating messages between agents as human approval. The docs say Claude Code is designed not to trust an "approved" claim relayed by another agent.

herdr.title: herdr
about: What it is. A terminal runtime built in Rust as a single binary. Its official description is "the runtime your coding agents live on"; it runs inside your existing terminal, and a background server keeps agent sessions alive. The GitHub organization is herdrdev, the site is herdr.dev, and the license is Apache-2.0.
It does not wrap agents; each runs as-is in its own terminal. Agents named in the docs are Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and Grok.
herdr.installCode:
curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh
# or
brew install herdr
mise use -g herdr
herdr.usage: Start it with herdr; running it again reattaches to the existing session. The default prefix key is ctrl+b (tmux style). Work continues even after you detach with ctrl+b q.
herdr.cliLead: An agent can create, read, and wait on other panes.
herdr.cliCode:
herdr workspace create --cwd ~/project --label api
herdr pane split w1:p1 --direction right
herdr pane run w1:p2 "npm test"
herdr pane read w1:p2 --source recent --lines 50
herdr agent wait w1:p1 --until done
herdr.cliNote: agent wait also accepts --until blocked. The socket API also has methods such as worktree.create, agent.prompt, and agent.wait. A skill that teaches agents this usage is installed like this:
herdr.skillNote: The skill has a safety rule that it must work only inside a herdr pane where HERDR_ENV=1 is set. An example of starting an agent inside herdr is herdr claude.
herdr.remote: You see saved SSH machines together with local work, and the server keeps the terminals alive even if the connection drops. If the server or machine restarts, the original processes do not survive; the saved layout is restored and supported agent sessions can be resumed.

orca.title: Orca
about: What it is. An open-source (MIT) desktop app made by Stably AI (the stablyai GitHub organization); the site is onorca.dev. It runs each agent in its own git worktree and says it is compatible with "any CLI agent".
Agents named include Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Amp, and Pi. There are desktop builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux, and mobile apps for iOS and Android.
orca.installWarn: The README warns you to use the full cask name. Using just orca points to an unrelated Plotly cask.
orca.usage: Give a big task to a coordinator agent and it starts worker agents, each in its own workspace. In the app you view diffs and leave notes on changed lines to send feedback to the agent. Agents, terminals, browsers, and diffs are arranged in split panels. You can also work on SSH hosts.
orca.cliLead: The app provides a CLI, which you register under Settings → General → Orca CLI.
orca.cliCode:
orca status --json
orca worktree create --repo id:<repoId> --name my-task --issue 123 --json
orca worktree ps --json
orca terminal send --text "continue" --enter --json
orca terminal wait --for tui-idle --timeout-ms 30000 --json
orca.skillNote: A skill that teaches agents how to use the CLI is installed with this command:

compare.title: herdr vs Orca

rows: Panes and workspaces, with a worktree method
A worktree per agent by default
tmux-like persistence and SSH, an API to wait on agent state
Diff review, issue/PR integration, a CLI to control the browser and emulator

compare.note: What they share is that an agent can start other agents through the CLI, and that is the point where you pass from "a person managing windows" to "agents managing agents". This research has no basis for saying either is better. Try them on one project and judge for yourself whether herdr suits terminal-centered work and Orca suits review- and GUI-centered work.

google.title: Note on the Google family
google.body: On 2026-05-19 Google announced the transition from Gemini CLI to Antigravity CLI (agy). Agent Skills, Hooks, Subagents, and Extensions (Antigravity plugins) carry over, and Google said there is no one-to-one feature parity at launch. Gemini CLI service for personal accounts (Google AI Pro, Ultra, and free) ended on 2026-06-18. So the Gemini CLI subagent information here is for existing users only. Antigravity CLI installs on macOS and Linux with curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash and is checked with agy --version. Run it with agy; agy -p "<prompt>" runs non-interactively, agy models lists models, and /plan inside a session asks for a plan first.

wrap.title: Wrap-up: what to try this week
steps: Step ②: create a small AGENTS.md (or a per-tool instruction file) in the repository and write three verification command lines.
Step ③: for your next feature, get a plan first, approve it, and then execute.
Step ⑤: split two independent tasks with git worktree and run them in two sessions.
When you feel friction up to this point, pick just one ⑥ tool and try it on one project.

mcp.description: The standard protocol AI agents use to reach external tools and data
mcp.conceptDesc: MCP is a standard protocol that connects AI agents to external systems such as databases, browsers, and external APIs. An MCP server provides tools (functions the agent can run), resources (data it can read), and prompts (reusable prompts), and the agent (the client) calls them. Local processes connect over stdio, and remote servers connect over Streamable HTTP.

mcp.specIntro: The latest revision of the MCP spec is 2026-07-28. Compared with the previous revision (2025-11-25), the basic structure of the protocol changed, so check the revision when you build a server or follow an older example.

items.title: Stateless protocol
items.before: The initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header were used.
items.after: The initialize handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone, and every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta.

items.title: server/discover added
items.after: An RPC that advertises the versions and capabilities a server supports, which servers must implement.

items.title: Tasks split out
items.before: Tasks were part of the core protocol as an experimental feature.
items.after: Tasks moved out of the core protocol into an official extension.

items.title: Roots, Sampling, Logging
items.before: Roots, Sampling, and Logging were active features.
items.after: They are deprecated. They keep working during the deprecation window, but new implementations should not use them.

items.title: HTTP+SSE transport
items.before: The HTTP+SSE transport had already been deprecated since the 2025-03-26 revision, but was not classified under a lifecycle policy.
items.after: The HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated and should be migrated to Streamable HTTP. stdio stays as is.

mcpServers.description: As of 2026-11-10: the MCP servers frontend developers actually connect, how to add them per agent, how usage has changed, and security rules.

intro.title: Why MCP is still used
intro.body: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that lets coding agents call tools and data from external services in a uniform way. A server provides Tools, Resources, and Prompts. In frontend work you mostly connect it for things like "reading Figma designs", "finding the latest library docs", "seeing errors from the running app", and "checking the screen in a browser". See the previous section for the concept and architecture.
intro.limitNote: MCP is not a cure-all, though. Because of token cost, handling the same jobs with a CLI plus skills has also become established. It is not a choice of one or the other but a matter of mixing them to fit the situation.
intro.basisBody: Server names, addresses, commands, and config keys are listed only where they were confirmed in each provider's official docs or official repository. "Widely used" here is not a ranking: it means the official docs provide separate install instructions for the major agents.

catalog.title: Servers by category
catalog.hint: Do not install every server. Starting with "docs search + browser + the server for your framework" is enough.

categories.title: Design, docs, repositories

rows.name: Figma MCP (remote)
rows.what: Generates code from a selected frame, extracts design context such as variables, components, and layout, keeps consistency with Code Connect, writes to the canvas (remote only)
rows.when: When turning a mockup into code

rows.name: Context7
rows.what: Resolves a library name to an ID (`resolve-library-id`) and fetches that library's docs (`query-docs`)
rows.when: When you want to stop the agent from using outdated APIs

rows.name: GitHub MCP
rows.what: Provides toolsets for working with repositories, issues, pull requests, and more
rows.when: When handing issue reading and PR work to the agent

notes: Figma also has a desktop server that goes through the desktop app, but the official docs recommend the remote server. The desktop server is for specific organization and enterprise needs and requires a Dev or Full seat.
GitHub MCP has `--toolsets` to choose tool groups and `--read-only` to remove write tools. Start with read-only.

categories.title: Deployment, error monitoring, backend

rows.name: Vercel MCP
rows.what: Docs search, project and deployment management, deployment log analysis, Web Analytics queries. A remote server using OAuth
rows.when: When investigating why a deployment failed together with the agent

rows.name: Sentry MCP
rows.what: Error search, performance analysis, issue triage, reading docs, project management. All connections use OAuth
rows.address: `https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp` (path to narrow to an organization and project: `/mcp/{organizationSlug}/{projectSlug}`)
rows.when: When tying production errors to code and fixing them

rows.name: Supabase MCP
rows.what: Provides tool groups such as database and docs
rows.when: Projects that use a Supabase backend

notes: For Supabase you can add `project_ref=<id>` (limit to one project), `read_only=true` (run as a read-only Postgres user), and `features=<group>` (limit the tool groups) to the address. Example: `https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp?project_ref=abc123&read_only=true`. The official docs treat this server as a tool that runs with developer privileges and warn you not to give it to customers or end users.

categories.title: Browser and debugging

rows.name: Chrome DevTools MCP
rows.what: Records performance traces with insights, analyzes network requests, takes screenshots, shows console messages with source-mapped stack traces, Puppeteer-based automation
rows.when: When checking in a real Chrome why a page is slow or broken

rows.name: Playwright MCP
rows.what: Opens a browser, reads the page structure, and operates it
rows.when: Exploratory automation, repeated checks that need persistent state

notes: Chrome DevTools MCP collects usage statistics by default, and its performance tools may send trace URLs to the Chrome UX Report API. You can turn these off with the `--no-usage-statistics` and `--no-performance-crux` options. Also, `--slim` is a reduced tool set for basic browser tasks.

The Playwright repository itself says that exposing the CLI as a skill is "more token-efficient" for coding agents, and describes MCP as suited to specialized loops that need persistent state and rich inspection. It is an example of one provider documenting both approaches.

categories.title: MCP servers provided directly by frameworks and UI libraries

rows.name: next-devtools-mcp
rows.what: Connects to the `/_next/mcp` endpoint of a Next.js 16+ dev server. Queries current errors, routes, logs, and compile problems, and points to docs matching the installed version
rows.when: When fixing errors with your Next.js app running on the dev server

rows.name: shadcn MCP
rows.what: Searches and installs components from registries. Private and third-party registries can be connected

rows.name: Storybook MCP
rows.what: Lets the agent reuse existing components and docs, write stories, and run story tests including accessibility
rows.when: When you manage a design system with Storybook

rows.name: MUI MCP
rows.what: A server that helps with using MUI

rows.name: Angular CLI MCP
rows.what: Starting and stopping the dev server, waiting for builds, best practices, docs search, and more

rows.name: Svelte MCP
rows.what: Tools based on the official docs and static analysis to catch common mistakes of generative AI

notes: The advantage of framework servers is that they see the state of "my app running right now", which a general docs search server cannot give you. Next.js `/_next/mcp` is on by default and can be turned off by setting `experimental.mcpServer` to `false` in `next.config`.

install.title: How to add a server per agent
install.hint: We use one remote server (Vercel) and one local server (Playwright) as examples. These are the formats confirmed in each tool's official docs.

items.name: Claude Code

blocks.code:
claude mcp add --transport http vercel https://mcp.vercel.com
claude mcp add --transport stdio airtable -- npx -y airtable-mcp-server
claude mcp list

bullets: Everything after `--` is the server launch command. Authenticate with `/mcp` inside a session, or `claude mcp login <name>` from the shell.

Scopes are local (default, `~/.claude.json`), project (`.mcp.json` in the repository, shared with the team), and user (`~/.claude.json`, all projects). Add settings you want to share with the team using `--scope project`.
A remote server entry in `.mcp.json` uses `"type": "http"` and `"url"`. An entry with only `url` and no `type` is treated as stdio and skipped.
Servers in `.mcp.json` ask for approval in interactive sessions. Environment variables can be inserted as `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}`.

blocks.code:
codex mcp add vercel --url https://mcp.vercel.com
codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp
codex mcp login <server-name>

blocks.note: The config file is `~/.codex/config.toml` (`.codex/config.toml` for trusted projects), and servers go in a `[mcp_servers.<name>]` table. stdio uses `command` and `args`, remote uses `url`.

items.name: Cursor
items.intro: The config file is `.cursor/mcp.json` in the project or the global `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, and the top-level key is `mcpServers`.
items.outro: If the remote server supports OAuth, the login flow starts without extra configuration. If you need a fixed client ID, add an `auth` object. You can also install from the Cursor Marketplace with "Add to Cursor".

items.name: GitHub Copilot / VS Code
items.intro: Run `MCP: Add Server` from the command palette, choose HTTP or Command (stdio), and choose where to save it, global or workspace. Unlike other tools, the top-level key in `.vscode/mcp.json` is `servers`.
items.outro: The VS Code docs describe `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` (or `$COPILOT_HOME/mcp-config.json`) as the global setting for Copilot and `.mcp.json` at the workspace root (requires the experimental setting `chat.mcp.workspaceRootConfig.enabled`) for sharing with the team, and mark the `.vscode/mcp.json` approach as "deprecated but still usable". This may change by version, so check the docs for the VS Code version you use.

items.name: Google family: Gemini CLI and Antigravity
bullets: Gemini CLI: write under `mcpServers` in `~/.gemini/settings.json` (user) or `.gemini/settings.json` (project). The keys are `command` for stdio, `url` for SSE, and `httpUrl` for Streamable HTTP. The command is `gemini mcp add --transport http <name> <url>`. The Gemini CLI docs note that, from 2026-06-18, for free-tier and Google One users it has been replaced by the Antigravity CLI.

Antigravity (2.0, shared by IDE and CLI): global `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`, workspace `.agents/mcp_config.json`. Remote entries use `serverUrl` (or `url`) and support Streamable HTTP only. The docs have no CLI "add" command; you open the manager screen with `/mcp` in the prompt or edit the file directly. MCP tools that are not configured default to Ask mode, which asks for approval before running.

items.name: Install to several agents at once
items.intro: The Vercel and Next.js docs point to the `add-mcp` CLI. It detects the installed agents and adds the server to each one's config.

blocks.code:
npx add-mcp https://mcp.vercel.com
npx add-mcp next-devtools-mcp@latest

items.title: Remote (HTTP) servers and OAuth are the default
items.body: Figma, Vercel, Sentry, Supabase, Context7, GitHub, and Svelte all provide remote addresses. Instead of downloading and running a package locally, registering an address and logging in from the browser has become common. The server then works with your account's permissions. The Vercel docs state that once connected, the AI system has "the same access permissions as your Vercel account".

items.title: Latest spec revision 2026-07-28
items.body: The latest revision of the official spec is 2026-07-28, and the previous one is 2025-11-25. The previous section covered the changes: the protocol became stateless, and Roots, Sampling, Logging, and the HTTP+SSE transport became Deprecated. Among these, for OAuth client registration, Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) became Deprecated and the Client ID Metadata Document is recommended; Vercel MCP also says it supports CIMD. Deprecated features get a deprecation grace period of at least 12 months. Also note that the spec versions that server docs refer to differ. For example, the Vercel docs say its implementation is based on the 2025-06-18 spec. Users usually need not care about this difference, but when you build a server yourself you must check which revision your SDK version supports.

items.title: Registry
items.body: The official MCP Registry collects metadata (`server.json`) of public servers and is still a preview ("breaking changes or data resets may occur"). Server names use reverse-DNS format such as `io.github.user/server-name`, and go through GitHub account or domain ownership verification. The official docs explain that the registry is designed to be used by downstream aggregators such as marketplaces rather than directly by host apps. The registry does not do security checks; it leaves them to package registries such as npm and to aggregators. So "it is in the registry" does not mean "it is safe".
bullets: There are also per-agent directories. The Claude Code docs point to the Anthropic Directory (`https://claude.ai/directory`), Cursor to the Cursor Marketplace, and VS Code to the Customization Marketplace (preview).

items.title: Deferred tool loading (tool search)
items.body: Putting every tool definition into the context up front wastes tokens. In Claude Code, Tool Search is on by default: it defers MCP tool definitions and loads them with `ToolSearch` when needed (turn it off with `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false`). So connecting several servers no longer burdens the context as much as before. Cutting the number of tools yourself still works too, for example with `--toolsets` in GitHub MCP or `features=` in Supabase.

items.title: CLI + skills instead of MCP
items.body: The Playwright repository itself says that using the CLI as a skill is more token-efficient for coding agents. Chrome DevTools MCP ships a `chrome-devtools` CLI and skills together, and Context7 lets you pick either a "CLI + Skills" mode or an "MCP" mode through the `ctx7` CLI. Next.js says that skills such as `next-dev-loop` call `/_next/mcp` directly. Blog benchmarks give varying figures, such as the CLI being 4 to 32 times cheaper, and many have a stake in the result, so it is better not to trust the numbers. Just remember these practical rules.
bullets: For services that need authentication, multi-user permissions, or organizational controls (Figma, Sentry, GitHub, etc.), remote MCP is more convenient.
For stateless jobs that finish in one command, or jobs that already have a CLI, CLI + skills is lighter.
Many tools offer both, so follow the one the official docs recommend.

items.title: Calling MCP through code execution
items.body: Anthropic's engineering article (2025-11-04) proposes presenting MCP servers as code APIs such as TypeScript modules and having the agent write code to call them. Because intermediate results are filtered in the execution environment and only what is needed goes to the model, the article's example says 150,000 tokens dropped to 2,000 tokens (a figure for that one workflow). The trade-off is that you need infrastructure such as a sandbox and resource limits. Ordinary users rarely set this up themselves, but it helps you understand the direction of "find and use tools when needed".

items.title: MCP Apps and extensions
items.body: MCP Apps is an extension where a server returns, along with the tool result, an interactive HTML UI (charts, forms, dashboards) that is rendered inside the conversation. `_meta.ui.resourceUri` in the tool description points to a `ui://` resource, and the host renders it in a sandboxed iframe and communicates via `postMessage`. The official docs list Claude, Claude Desktop, VS Code GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Goose, and others as supported clients. For frontend developers, what matters is that "the results of an MCP server can be drawn with web technologies (React, Vue, Svelte, etc.)". Extensions are optional features used only when both server and client support them. Tasks and Skills over MCP are also introduced as official extensions.

security.title: Security
items: The official spec treats tools as arbitrary code execution and says not to trust tool descriptions and annotations unless they come from a trusted server. The host must obtain user consent before calling a tool.

Prompt injection: an agent may follow instructions hidden in external text such as issues, logs, and support tickets. The Supabase and Vercel docs warn of the same risk and tell you to keep human confirmation on.
security.incidentsBody: On 2025-12-17, GitHub security advisories disclosed three vulnerabilities in Anthropic's reference Git MCP server (`mcp-server-git`): CVE-2025-68143, CVE-2025-68144, and CVE-2025-68145. The `git_init` tool could create a repository at any path, `git_diff` and `git_checkout` had argument injection, and the `--repository` option lacked path validation. They were fixed in versions 2025.9.25 or 2025.12.18, and the `git_init` tool was removed. In Cursor, CVE-2025-54136 let an already-trusted MCP configuration file be modified in versions 1.2.4 and below so that code ran without re-approval; it was fixed in 1.3.
security.practicesHint: Tick each rule as you adopt it.
practices: Confirm the address is official, and check the domain of one-click install links on marketplaces.
Limit to read-only and project scope where possible (`read_only=true`, `project_ref`, `--read-only`).
Connect production data only when needed.
Do not turn off tool-call approval.
Do not write tokens directly in a `.mcp.json` committed to the repository; use environment variables.
Do not download and run a `.mcp.json` that someone else uploaded without reviewing it.

start.title: Recommended order to get started
start.hint: Click a step to jump, or use Previous and Next.
steps: Connect Context7 to reduce the outdated API problem.
Connect the official server of the framework you use (`next-devtools-mcp` for Next.js).
Pick just one of Chrome DevTools MCP or Playwright for verifying the screen.
If your team uses Figma, connect the Figma remote server.
When needed, add GitHub, Vercel, and Sentry, mostly for reading.
Check the connected servers periodically with a command like `claude mcp list` and remove the ones you do not use.

hooks.title: Hooks: Event-Driven Automation
hooks.infoDesc: A hook is a handler that runs automatically when a lifecycle event occurs in the agent. Instructions in CLAUDE.md are only context the agent consults, but a hook always runs when its condition matches, so hooks are how you enforce rules that can't have exceptions. A command hook receives the event data as JSON on stdin, and returning exit code 2 blocks the action. Note that any other error code, including 1, is treated as a non-blocking error and the action still proceeds.

events.name: SessionStart
events.timing: When a session starts or resumes

events.name: UserPromptSubmit
events.timing: Right after a prompt is submitted, before processing

events.name: Notification
events.usage: Forwarding to desktop or chat notifications

hooks.note: There are more than 30 events in total, including SubagentStop, SessionEnd, and PermissionRequest. Besides shell commands (command), hook types include http, mcp_tool, prompt, and the experimental agent.

sim.title: Exit Code Simulator
sim.hint: Pick the exit code a command hook script returns to see what happens to the action. The scenario is block-rm.sh from the script example meeting an rm -rf command.
sim.label: Choose an exit code

results.text: Treated as a normal exit, so the action proceeds.
The action is blocked. block-rm.sh prints "rm -rf is blocked by a hook" to stderr and returns exit 2.
Any other error code, including 1, is treated as a non-blocking error and the action still proceeds. exit 1 does not block.

hooks.scriptCode:
#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/format.sh — input arrives as JSON on stdin
FILE=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path')
npx prettier --write "$FILE"

#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/block-rm.sh
COMMAND=$(jq -r '.tool_input.command')
if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then
  echo "rm -rf is blocked by a hook" >&2
  exit 2   # 2 = block. exit 1 does not block
fi
exit 0

claudeMd.title: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md: Project Context
claudeMd.infoDesc: CLAUDE.md is a project instruction file loaded at the start of every session. Put in it what can't be learned from the code alone: build and test commands, code conventions, and rules that must be followed. It always takes up context, so keep it under 200 lines, move procedures needed only for specific tasks into skills, and move rules that apply only to certain paths into .claude/rules/. The /init command generates a first draft. If you use several tools, keep the instructions in the standard AGENTS.md file. Claude Code (v2.1.277 or later) reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md, and reads only CLAUDE.md when both exist.

agentMode.subAgentsInfoTitle: Helpers that work in their own context
agentMode.subAgentsInfoDesc: A subagent works in a context separate from the main conversation and returns only a summarized result. Hand it tasks with long output, such as exploration or test runs, and the main context stays clean. Define roles you use often as Markdown files under .claude/agents/ and reuse them.

The agent asks multiple-choice questions about each undecided part, then writes up a spec document once the answers add up.

browserAutomation.description: A map of the tools for handing a browser to an agent, grouped by category. The reference date is 2026-11-10, and the content centers on what was verified in official docs and repositories. For ego and aside it also includes what we confirmed by running them.

overview.title: The Big Picture: Which Browser Does the Agent Use?
overview.lead: When you hand a browser to an agent, the first questions are not about tool names. They are these two.
axes: Does the agent use my real logged-in browser, or a clean separate browser?
Does the agent see the page as text (an accessibility snapshot) or as an image (screenshot + coordinates)?
overview.tableLead: Along these two axes, the tools fall into roughly five categories.

categories.title: (1) Browsers and extensions shared by human and agent
categories.tools: Aside, ego(lite), Claude in Chrome, ChatGPT browser extension
categories.detailTitle: (1) Browsers and extensions from AI companies

items.name: Claude in Chrome
items.desc: Became generally available on all paid plans on 2026-08-26. You install it from the Chrome Web Store and it is Chrome only (other Chromium browsers and mobile are not supported). It can also run autonomously without approval for each action. It reportedly uses training, web-content detection probes, and a pre-execution classifier against prompt injection, but this is Anthropic's own evaluation, so treat it as reference only. In Claude Code, start with claude --chrome, or run /chrome inside a session to check the connection and reconnect. It needs extension 1.0.36 or later and a /login sign-in; with API key or setup-token authentication, the Chrome integration stays off.

items.name: ChatGPT
items.desc: The standalone Atlas browser was deprecated; OpenAI's help page says it is moving browser-based agentic capabilities into ChatGPT and Codex, and points to the ChatGPT Chrome extension or sidebar for help in Chrome. The desktop app's built-in browser uses a separate profile and does not share existing sessions; OpenAI's docs say to use the browser extension for Chrome/Edge/Brave and others when you need logged-in sites.

items.name: Gemini in Chrome (auto browse)
items.desc: Google's blog says auto browse is available only to Google AI Pro/Ultra subscribers in the U.S. Gemini in Chrome asks for confirmation before sensitive actions such as sending an email or adding a calendar event.

categories.hint: Aside and ego are covered in detail right below, in "The Two Stars".

categories.title: (2) CLIs called from the shell

items.name: playwright-cli
items.desc: npm install -g @playwright/cli. A CLI for coding agents; the official docs say it keeps token cost low by not loading tool schemas and verbose accessibility trees into context. It has commands like open, snapshot, click, and fill, -s=<name> sessions, and a daemon model. To connect to a running browser, use one of playwright-cli attach --extension=chrome (needs the Playwright extension, Chrome/Edge only), attach --cdp=chrome (a running Chrome/Edge), or attach --cdp=<url> (a CDP endpoint); playwright-cli detach drops only the connection and leaves the external browser running.

items.name: agent-browser (vercel-labs, Apache-2.0)
items.desc: npm install -g agent-browser, then agent-browser install. agent-browser open example.com, agent-browser snapshot -i (refs like @e1 on interactive elements), agent-browser click @e1. The README says a background daemon controls Chrome for Testing over CDP, and that you can attach to a running Chrome with --cdp/--auto-connect.

items.name: chrome-devtools CLI
items.desc: npm i chrome-devtools-mcp@latest -g, then use it as chrome-devtools <tool> ... The default is headless, isolated mode.

categories.note: Shared traits: each command returns a short piece of text, so less context piles up.

categories.title: (3) MCP servers
categories.tools: Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP, aside mcp
categories.login: A separate profile by default, with an option to connect to an existing Chrome

items.name: Playwright MCP
items.desc: npx @playwright/mcp@latest. Accessibility snapshots are the default, and --caps=vision adds coordinate-based tools. The default is a persistent per-workspace profile, and --isolated uses an in-memory profile. --extension lets you reuse the logged-in session of an existing Chrome/Edge. Install the Playwright extension from the Chrome Web Store and add --extension to args in the MCP config; the first time the LLM uses the browser, a page opens where you choose which tab it can control. Putting PLAYWRIGHT_MCP_EXTENSION_TOKEN from the extension's status page into env skips the approval prompt. The README summarizes that CLI+skills are token-efficient and preferred for coding agents, while MCP suits persistent state, rich page inspection, and long-running autonomous work. It also states that it is 'not a security boundary'.

items.name: Chrome DevTools MCP
items.desc: npx -y chrome-devtools-mcp@latest. Its strength is debugging: performance traces, network, and console stack traces with source maps applied. The only officially supported browsers are Chrome and Chrome for Testing. You can attach to a running Chrome session with --autoConnect (Chrome 144 or later, allow it at chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging, a permission dialog on every connection, and a banner while being controlled). This is based on a Chrome blog post, so current details may have changed. Usage statistics collection is on by default and can be turned off with --no-usage-statistics.

categories.note: MCP tool schemas stay resident in context, so the more tools there are, the higher the baseline cost (the comparison table in the Playwright docs also lists MCP token cost as "Higher").

categories.title: (4) Browsers built into coding agents and IDEs
categories.tools: Cursor browser, ChatGPT/Codex app built-in browser
categories.view: Screenshots, console and network logs, etc.
categories.detailTitle: (4) Browsers built into coding agents and IDEs

items.name: Cursor
items.desc: Opens as a window inside the editor and is controlled by an MCP server (extension). It can navigate, click, type, take screenshots, and inspect the console and network, and cookies and storage persist between agent sessions but are isolated per workspace. The agent is prompted to detect running dev servers and use the right port, and admins can limit automatic navigation with an allowlist of origins such as http://localhost:3000. Approval is required by default, and the docs call the allow/block lists 'best-effort protection'. It advises against auto-run on unfamiliar sites.

items.name: ChatGPT app built-in browser
items.desc: The user and the agent look at the same screen, can preview local or public pages, and can leave visual comments. It uses a separate profile, so you log in yourself. Developer mode (full CDP access) is an opt-in that requires explicit per-site approval.

categories.note: This is the category frontend developers use most often. For checking a local dev server that needs no login, this alone is often enough.

items.name: Browserbase / Stagehand
items.desc: Browserbase provides headless cloud browsers and session observation (logs, live view, replay), and Stagehand is an SDK that adds act/extract/observe on top of Playwright-level control. It suits service operation (collection, large-scale parallelism) and is overkill for checking screens during development. You connect the connectUrl returned when you create a session with Playwright's chromium.connectOverCDP(session.connectUrl). Contexts store cookies, session tokens, and local storage; pass { id, persist: true } as browserSettings.context when creating a session, and any session with the same context ID starts logged in.

items.name: Claude computer use
items.desc: It works with screenshots and mouse/keyboard coordinates. The API docs say you enable it with the single line {"type": "computer_toolset_20260801"}, that it has 17 component tools, and that browser tools are better for tasks that stay inside a web page. The docs state that one screenshot costs roughly 1,000 to 1,800 input tokens. The security recommendations are a dedicated VM/container, not providing sensitive information, a domain allowlist, and human confirmation before important actions.

items.name: Prompt injection
items.desc: Text on a web page can be read by the agent as a command. The OpenAI, Cursor, and Anthropic docs all say to treat page content as untrusted input. No defense metric is a guarantee that 'no incident will happen'.

items.name: Real account permissions
items.desc: The extension/autoConnect approaches in (1) and (3) mean the agent can reach mail, payments, and admin screens through your session. Do not use a profile that mixes work and personal accounts as is; keep a separate profile for agent work.

items.name: Recommendations
items.desc: Start with read-mostly tasks, have a human approve payments, deletions, posting, and permission changes, and keep auth files and tokens out of the repository. Do not let the agent bypass confirmation dialogs.

duo.title: The Two Stars: ego and aside

ego.name: ego
ego.title: ego (ego lite, ego-browser)
ego.code:
# Install only the skill first
npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite

# Import your Chrome login state
ego-browser import list
ego-browser import --browser chrome --profile Default

# Other commands
ego-browser skill      # print the skill guide
ego-browser upgrade
sections: A free Chromium-based browser built by Citro Labs. It is designed so that a human and an AI agent can work in the same browser without fighting over control. The CLI is named ego-browser.

Per the official repository (citrolabs/ego-lite), download and run the installer for macOS (Apple Silicon/Intel) or Windows, and the ego-browser skill is installed into the agent's skills directory along with it. To add only the skill first, use npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite; the agent's first browser task then walks you through installing the app. Linux is only on the roadmap. The repository contents are MIT-licensed, and the browser app is distributed separately for free.
On first launch it asks whether to import your Chrome logins, cookies, extensions, and bookmarks. You can also import from the CLI, and after importing, the agent inherits that logged-in state.

When the agent passes JavaScript to ego-browser nodejs, it runs in the browser's built-in Node.js runtime. The script runs in Node, not inside the page, so code that must run inside the page goes into page.evaluate().
Each agent task gets an isolated workspace called a Space, and the user's existing tabs are left alone. The user can watch the agent work and take over at any time (task.handOff()).
For observing the page there are page.snapshot() (structure and refs, the default tool) and page.screenshot() (visual check). You act on refs from the snapshot, such as @21, like page.click("@21").

It looks like Playwright but is not Playwright. The skill document explicitly says not to guess at Playwright APIs such as locator() or getByRole(). Anything not in the list is handled with page.evaluate() or page.cdp().

Token cost profile: The skill document recommends using only the one of snapshot or screenshot you need, batching several actions into one script, and taking a single snapshot at the end. In other words, it is designed to cut round trips.

The content of the pages the agent works on is sent to the model the user selected (official site). Because it uses your real logged-in session, whatever the agent can do is whatever your account can do.

aside.name: aside
aside.title: aside
aside.code:
# macOS install (developer docs)
curl -fsSL https://releases.aside.com/install.sh | bash

# Login: set the auth file path first, then approve the code in the browser under Settings > Account > Devices
export ASIDE_CLI_AUTH_PATH="/absolute/path/aside-auth.json"
aside login --email "you@example.com"

aside "smoke test localhost:3000"   # natural-language task
aside repl "const p = await openTab('https://example.com')"   # deterministic step
aside mcp                                     # stdio MCP server
sections: A 'browser rebuilt for humans and agents' made by Aside Computer Inc. (a Y Combinator company). Its core message is working on logged-in sites without integrations.
It supports macOS 15 or later and Windows 10 22H2 or later / Windows 11.

Onboarding imports browsing history, cookies, and bookmarks from Chrome and others. The official site says the agent logs in through autofill so credentials are not exposed to the agent, and that sensitive actions such as payments, posting, and messaging wait for user confirmation.
Other commands: aside session resume <session-id> "Continue", aside account list/status/use. The auth file is set with ASIDE_CLI_AUTH_PATH; if unset, ~/.aside/cli/auth.json is used.
An outside agent has two ways in. aside exec hands the whole task to the Aside agent inside the browser; the CLI guide recommends treating it like spawning a subagent.
aside repl drives tabs directly with Playwright-style JavaScript, where snapshot() is the primary way to read a page and annotatedScreenshot() and page.screenshot() are for visual checks.
Coding agent integration: The developer docs (aside.com/developers.md) list three options: CLI, MCP, and REPL.

For MCP, in mcp.json under mcpServers set command to aside and args to ["mcp"]. Running aside mcp directly shows four tools: exec (run the browser agent on logged-in sites), repl (run Playwright-style JavaScript), memory_search (search the user memory Aside has built), and browser_profiles (list browser profiles).
With a curl | bash install, it is safer to read the script before running it. Never commit the auth file (the official docs give the same warning).

duo.compareTitle: What the Two Tools Share and Where They Differ
compareItems: Shared: both are 'browsers shared by human and agent' where the agent inherits your logged-in session. Both import Chrome data.

Different: ego centers on JS scripts that the outside agent writes itself (ego-browser nodejs). aside has its own agent inside the browser, so handing over the whole task with exec is the default and repl is for when you need direct control. A running task can be redirected or stopped with aside session steer, queue, and stop, and --permission (ask, guard, full-access) sets the permission scope. ego's skill repository is public (MIT), and for aside the CLI's aside guide plays the same role.

hook.title: Automatic Verification
hook.infoDesc: A PostToolUse hook can run lint or type checks every time a file is modified. When a check fails, exit with code 2 and write the errors to stderr; they are passed to the agent, which fixes them itself. To force the full test suite when the agent finishes, use a Stop hook.
hook.scriptCode:
#!/bin/bash
# .claude/hooks/lint-file.sh
FILE=$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path')
if ! npx eslint "$FILE" >&2; then
  exit 2   # the lint output (stderr) is passed back to the agent
fi

checklist.title: Manual Verification Checklist
items: Does the business logic match the requirements?
Is it consistent with existing code patterns?
Are there security vulnerabilities? (input validation, authn/authz)
Does it use packages or APIs that don't exist?
Are there performance problems? (N+1, memory leaks)
Is error handling appropriate?
Do the tests verify real behavior? (not tests written only to pass)

permissions.title: Permission Management
permissions.infoDesc: Write per-tool rules under permissions in settings.json to set what is allowed. Rules are evaluated in the order deny, ask, allow, and the first match decides the outcome, so an allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule. Commit them to the project's .claude/settings.json and the whole team uses the same rules.

status.skipped: Skipped because an earlier rule already matched

injection.title: Guarding Against Prompt Injection
injection.desc: Web pages, issue bodies, and MCP tool responses that the agent reads can hide instructions meant to trick it. Content that comes from outside must be treated as data, not instructions, and you should not install MCP servers, skills, or plugins from unknown sources. Block files that hold secrets with deny rules, and use bypassPermissions mode, which skips all checks, only in isolated environments.

tokenOptimization.description: Habits that keep context small to manage cost and quality together
tokenOptimization.contextOptimizationInfoTitle: The basic principle for cutting cost
tokenOptimization.contextOptimizationInfoDesc: Token cost scales with context size. The agent resends the whole conversation with every request, so in a session left open all day, even a one-line question is processed together with everything accumulated so far. Keeping context small is the most effective saving.
contextOptimizationChecklist: Start fresh with /clear when you move to unrelated work
Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, and move task-specific instructions into skills
Hand tasks with long output, such as test runs or log analysis, to subagents
For tools that have a CLI (gh, aws, and so on), use the CLI instead of MCP, and turn off unused MCP servers
Handle most work with a lighter model, and save the top model and high effort for complex design
Vague requests trigger broad exploration. Spell out the files, scope, and done criteria
If the direction is wrong, stop right away with Esc and go back with /rewind
